Lab Practical • Microbiology

Gram Staining

Principles, cell-wall anatomy, laboratory procedure, microscopic interpretation, troubleshooting and quality control.

Method: Differential bacteriological stain Discovered: Hans Christian Gram, 1884 Brightfield: 1000× oil immersion Typical staining time: 3–5 min

Visual Diagrams from the Gram Staining Reference

The three reference figures are included here so the practical section is complete on mobile and desktop.

1. Principle

Gram staining differentiates bacteria according to differences in their cell-envelope structure and their ability to retain the crystal-violet–iodine complex during decolorization.

Key idea: Gram-positive cells retain the crystal-violet–iodine complex and appear purple; Gram-negative cells lose the complex during decolorization and take the counterstain, appearing pink/red.

2. Gram-Positive Cell Envelope

  • Thick peptidoglycan layer: about 20–80 nm.
  • Multiple peptidoglycan sheets form a strong wall.
  • Wall teichoic acid and lipoteichoic acid are present.
  • Outer membrane and LPS are absent.
  • The thick wall dehydrates and its pores become smaller during alcohol treatment, helping retain the dye complex.

3. Gram-Negative Cell Envelope

  • Thin peptidoglycan layer: about 2–7 nm.
  • Outer membrane is present.
  • Outer leaflet contains lipopolysaccharide (LPS).
  • Periplasmic space is relatively expansive.
  • Porin proteins are present in the outer membrane.
  • Alcohol disrupts the lipid-rich outer membrane, allowing the crystal-violet–iodine complex to escape.

4. Four Reagents and Their Functions

Mobile view: swipe left/right inside the table when a column is wider than the screen.
StepReagentFunctionExpected colour
1Crystal violetPrimary stain; enters bacterial cells and produces the initial violet colour.G(+) violet; G(−) violet
2Gram's iodineMordant; forms the crystal-violet–iodine complex.Both dark purple
395% ethanol or ethanol–acetoneDecolorizer; differentiates the two cell-envelope types.G(+) retains purple; G(−) becomes colourless
4Safranin OCounterstain; colours decolorized cells pink/red.G(+) purple; G(−) pink/red

5. Laboratory Procedure

1 • Crystal violetFlood smear for 60 s, then gently rinse with water for 2–3 s.
2 • IodineFlood with Gram's iodine for 60 s, then gently rinse.
3 • DecolorizeApply 95% ethanol or acetone-alcohol for about 10–20 s; stop immediately with water.
4 • CounterstainFlood with safranin for 45–60 s, rinse, blot gently and air-dry.
Smear preparation and fixation
  1. Use a clean, grease-free glass slide and label it.
  2. For solid culture, use a small drop of sterile 0.9% saline and emulsify an isolated colony.
  3. For broth culture, transfer 1–2 loopfuls directly.
  4. Prepare a thin, uniform smear and allow it to air-dry completely.
  5. Never heat a wet slide.
  6. Heat-fix the completely dry smear by passing it smear-side up through the blue cone of a Bunsen flame three times, about 1 second each.
Critical step — decolorization: This is the main differentiating step. Too much alcohol can make Gram-positive organisms appear falsely Gram-negative; too little can make Gram-negative organisms appear falsely Gram-positive.

6. Microscopy

  1. Examine the prepared slide under a compound light microscope.
  2. Initially scan at low power to assess smear density and host cellularity.
  3. Proceed to the 100× oil-immersion objective.
  4. Total magnification with a 10× eyepiece is approximately 1000×.

7. Common Morphology

  • G(+) cocci: purple spheres; may occur in clusters, chains or pairs.
  • G(+) bacilli: purple rods, including large boxcar rods and coryneform forms.
  • G(−) bacilli: pink/red rods, including enteric rods and curved rods.
  • G(−) cocci: pink/red diplococci; Neisseria may show kidney-bean-shaped paired cells.

8. Important Examples

CategoryTypical examplesCharacteristic appearance
G(+) cocciStaphylococcus aureus; Streptococcus pyogenes; Streptococcus pneumoniae; EnterococcusPurple cocci in clusters, chains or pairs.
G(+) bacilliBacillus; Clostridium; Corynebacterium; Listeria; Actinomyces; NocardiaPurple rods with characteristic shapes/arrangements.
G(−) bacilliEscherichia coli; Klebsiella; Proteus; Salmonella; Shigella; Pseudomonas; VibrioPink/red rods; arrangement and shape vary.
G(−) cocciNeisseria meningitidis; Neisseria gonorrhoeae; MoraxellaPink/red diplococci; Neisseria may be intracellular in PMNs.

9. Troubleshooting

  • Over-decolorization: prolonged alcohol exposure can falsely make Gram-positive cells pink.
  • Under-decolorization: inadequate alcohol exposure or a thick smear can falsely keep Gram-negative cells violet.
  • Old culture: cultures older than the recommended fresh-culture period may become Gram-variable because of cell-wall changes.
  • Overheating: excessive heat fixation can damage cells and create staining artifacts.
  • Old/unfiltered crystal violet: precipitated dye may be mistaken for bacteria.

10. Quality Control

  • Use known control organisms to verify the staining procedure.
  • Staphylococcus aureus ATCC 25923: expected Gram-positive cocci in clusters, purple.
  • Escherichia coli ATCC 25922: expected Gram-negative bacilli, pink/red.
  • Host leukocytes, epithelial cells, mucus and RBCs do not contain peptidoglycan and should not remain purple after proper decolorization.

11. Organisms Poorly Visualized by Standard Gram Staining

Organism/groupReasonPreferred method from the reference
MycobacteriumWaxy, mycolic-acid-rich envelope.Acid-fast staining; auramine/rhodamine fluorescence.
Mycoplasma / UreaplasmaLack a peptidoglycan cell wall.PCR/NAAT, serology or specialized media.
SpirochetesVery small diameter, below routine brightfield resolution.Darkfield or silver methods; serology where appropriate.
Chlamydia / RickettsiaObligate intracellular organisms with specialized structural biology.Giemsa, direct fluorescent methods and NAAT/PCR.
Legionella pneumophilaMay stain weakly with standard safranin in some specimens.Modified Gram stain with basic fuchsin and other specialized methods.

12. Quick Revision

Order: Crystal violet → Iodine → Alcohol/Acetone → Safranin.

Mnemonic: Come In And Stain — Crystal violet, Iodine, Alcohol/Acetone, Safranin.

Final result: Gram-positive = purple/deep violet; Gram-negative = pink/bright red.

Most critical technical variable: correct decolorization.

Reference: Practical sequence and visual concepts are based on the uploaded Gram Staining MLT Arena reference material.
